rationale: obs[S1]: AllMusic lists Funk, Fusion, Jazz-Funk, Modal Music, Post-Bop and Piano Jazz styles and records September 1973 sessions at Wally Heider and Different Fur, San Francisco. obs[S2]: Wikipedia documents the Headhunters quintet (Hancock, Maupin, Jackson, Mason, Summers), track listing, chart peaks (Billboard 200 No. 13, R&B/Hip-Hop No. 2) and Columbia release date October 26, 1973. obs[S3]: MusicBrainz release group confirms the identifier. inf: The album is the canonical bridge from Hancock's Blue Note post-bop and Mwandishi electric experiments into the jazz-funk pocket; it made the Headhunters lineup a template for the groove lineage. unk: Specific per-studio date is not broken down beyond 'September 1973'.
bridge_case: Connects Hancock's established post-bop and Mwandishi electric language (already in the canon's orbit) to the jazz-funk groove bands that followed, and from there to the funk/hip-hop sampling lineage the canon eventually reaches.
scope_flag: Fusion gate — groove-first, riff-based funk rhythm and synthesizer/Clavinet textures are the organizing language; the case-against is that its commercial crossover success can make it look like a pop record rather than a jazz lineage statement.

scope_check.boundary_note: The 1973–1979 continuity test and newly opened fusion gate are both in play: its funk vamps, backbeat, Clavinet, and synthesizers raise the question whether it extends Hancock's post-bop/modal and Mwandishi lineage or founds a separate instrumental-funk idiom.

ballot.case_for: Head Hunters is a defining jazz-funk statement and an exceptionally strong bridge record: Hancock and Mwandishi holdover Bennie Maupin carry the electric, modal, and post-bop experimentation of the 1960s into a durable groove language. The Hancock–Maupin–Paul Jackson–Harvey Mason–Bill Summers quintet created a self-contained template whose influence reaches later groove jazz and hip-hop-facing instrumental music; the dossier documents its major crossover reach (Billboard 200 No. 13; R&B No. 2) and its complete, stable personnel across the session (S2). "Chameleon" and the radically recast "Watermelon Man" also make it an unusually immediate discovery record: accessible without reducing the band's rhythmic invention or collective identity.
ballot.case_against: The album's organizing principle is locked funk rhythm, riff repetition, and electric keyboard texture rather than the interactive swing, harmonic movement, or modal improvisational space central to the canon's post-bebop core. On a strict reading of the 1973+ continuity rule, it does not extend that tradition in the manner of late modal ECM but crosses into commercially oriented instrumental funk, precisely the drift the fusion anti-drift note warns against. Its dossier establishes factual metadata but supplies no independent canon-list evidence—no Penguin, DownBeat, JazzTimes, NPR, or comparable critical source—so claims of overwhelming critical consensus should not be treated as sourced here.
ballot.disagreement: Both references tier it as a fusion/1973+ scope call and regard it as a defining jazz-funk record, but they differ over consensus evidence: one treats its canonical reputation as overwhelming, while the other correctly notes that the supplied sources document sales and metadata rather than independent critical-list consensus.
ballot.recommendation: The council proposes that John treat Head Hunters as a must-have if he judges its Mwandishi-to-jazz-funk bridge sufficiently continuous with the post-bebop tradition; otherwise, the fusion boundary should exclude it rather than its quality.
